paragraphs: Evaluating generated code requires checking both whether it works and whether it contains exploitable weaknesses. Security benchmarks have typically required substantial expert effort, yet they need continual renewal as existing tasks enter training data and models become more capable. AutoBaxBuilder addresses this maintenance problem by automatically creating new code security evaluation tasks.

The pipeline combines language models’ code understanding with reliability checks. It constructs functional tests alongside end-to-end exploits that probe security, making intended behavior and vulnerability detection part of the same task-building process. The authors assess its quality by comparing its predictions with an expert-written baseline and manually checking task soundness.

The resulting public benchmark, AutoBaxBench, accompanies an evaluation of contemporary language models. The authors report task generation in under two hours for less than four US dollars. Even when manual verification is included, benchmark construction requires twelve times less human effort. The contribution is therefore a practical way to refresh security evaluations while retaining explicit checks on the reliability of generated tasks.
icml-2026-autobaxbuilder-bootstrapping-c.tldr: AutoBaxBuilder automates security benchmark construction with functional tests and exploits, reducing human effort twelvefold including manual verification.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language models often relies on newly generated responses from the model currently being trained. Generating those responses can be expensive. This paper studies whether storing past rollouts and using them again, a practice called experience replay, can reduce that cost while retaining the benefits of post-training.

The authors frame replay-buffer design as a balance among three factors: older data can increase variance as the model changes, a useful training collection needs diversity, and producing fresh samples consumes computation. This formulation makes data freshness one consideration within a broader efficiency problem. Their analysis shows that strict on-policy sampling is suboptimal when generation is expensive.

Empirically, a well-designed replay buffer substantially reduces inference computation without lowering final model performance in the reported study; some cases improve performance. It also preserves policy entropy, a measure of how varied the model’s choices remain. These findings support selective reuse of training experience and make buffer design central to achieving the reported savings.
icml-2026-efficient-rl-training-for-llms.tldr: Carefully designed replay buffers reduce language-model RL generation costs while preserving, and sometimes improving, final performance.

paragraphs: Loss curvature describes how the training objective bends as model weights change. Many learning methods need this information, but representing and manipulating it becomes difficult for large neural networks. This paper uses weight-space symmetries, transformations that leave the loss unchanged, to impose useful structure on curvature approximations.

The method analytically averages over these transformations to construct approximate Hessians from individual gradients. The resulting structures can be estimated, stored, and inverted tractably. A user chooses the symmetry group, which controls the balance between computational expense and approximation accuracy. Symmetry therefore becomes a direct design choice for deciding how much curvature information to retain.

The framework also connects existing approaches: one symmetry choice produces curvature estimates resembling those used by Shampoo and Muon. The authors validate their method across network architectures and apply it to second-order optimization benchmarks, including a small language model. They identify uncertainty estimation, continual learning, compression, pruning, and training-data attribution as possible further applications; these are prospective uses rather than additional demonstrated results.
icml-2026-exploiting-weight-space-symmet.tldr: Weight-space symmetries yield tractable curvature approximations whose accuracy and cost depend on the chosen symmetry group.

paragraphs: Private hypothesis selection asks which candidate distribution best explains observed samples while satisfying differential privacy. The challenge is to obtain strong statistical accuracy without making selection computationally expensive. This paper introduces algorithms that achieve near-optimal statistical rates with running time nearly linear in the number of candidate hypotheses.

A major computational obstacle is scoring candidates through comparisons with other candidates. Applying the exponential mechanism directly to such scores can require substantial comparison work. The authors instead construct a loss using a small collection of strong hypotheses. That structure makes the score efficient to evaluate for most candidates, reducing the computational burden of private selection.

The algorithms also extend to the agnostic setting, where none of the candidate distributions need equal the true distribution. This broadens the selection problem beyond finding a correctly specified candidate. As an application, the authors obtain faster differentially private algorithms for universal statistical estimation in low dimensions. The contribution is a way to combine efficient computation with near-optimal statistical performance under a privacy requirement.
icml-2026-fast-and-near-optimal-algorith.tldr: A loss built from a small set of strong hypotheses enables nearly linear-time private selection with near-optimal statistical rates.

paragraphs: Model stitching evaluates whether representations from independently trained networks can be aligned to solve a task. Successful stitching is often treated as evidence that the networks learned similar input–output relationships. This paper examines a problem with that interpretation: networks can use different information cues while still producing representations that are compatible in the forward direction.

The authors trace the problem to invariance properties, which describe changes a model can ignore while maintaining its behavior. Standard stitching does not account for these properties. As a result, its compatibility test can overlook meaningful differences in what the original models depend on, even when the combined system successfully performs the task.

The proposed approach requires both forward and backward compatibility and formulates model stitching around invariance awareness. By analyzing key stitching configurations, the authors study how the two compatibility requirements interact. Their analysis reveals functional discrepancies hidden by conventional stitching and provides a more principled basis for evaluating similarity. The central contribution is a stronger interpretation of representation compatibility when assessing whether models actually behave alike.
icml-2026-grounding-functional-similarit.tldr: Invariance-aware model stitching adds forward–backward compatibility to reveal functional differences that standard stitching can miss.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent distributes learning across cooperating users. Convergence guarantees based on mean-squared error describe average behavior, while high-probability guarantees provide stronger control over individual runs. Previous decentralized analyses required restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded gradients or noise that eventually disappears, to establish the latter kind of guarantee.

This paper proves high-probability convergence in the presence of light-tailed noise using the same conditions on the cost function needed for mean-squared convergence. Its analysis gives order-optimal rates for both non-convex and strongly convex objectives. The noise assumption remains part of the result; the relaxation concerns the restrictive conditions imposed by earlier analyses.

The authors also establish linear speed-up with the number of users, with transient periods matching or improving on those from mean-squared analyses. Their technical tools explain a high-probability variance-reduction effect of decentralization and bound a moment-generating function for strongly convex costs. Numerical experiments support the theory. Together, the results connect reliable individual-run behavior with the efficiency benefits of adding participants.
icml-2026-high-probability-convergence-g.tldr: Under light-tailed noise, decentralized SGD achieves sharp high-probability convergence and linear user-count speed-up with relaxed cost-function assumptions.

paragraphs: Customizing a language model served through an API is difficult when its weights cannot be changed. Advisor Models move the trainable component outside that service: a small open-weight model learns to produce natural-language advice for each individual request. The frontier model then receives that advice through its available prompting interface.

Because advice changes with the instance, the method can tailor guidance to the problem or user preference at hand. The authors report a 27.4% performance improvement for GPT-5.2 on RuleArena’s Taxes task and 24.6% fewer steps for Gemini 3 Pro on software engineering agent tasks. For personalizing GPT-5, advisors achieve reported results of 85–100%, compared with 40–60% for static prompt optimizers.

An advisor trained using a lower-cost student also transfers improvements to a frontier model. The authors observe no degradation on other evaluated benchmarks outside the pipeline’s training target. These findings suggest that training a separate advice generator can provide practical customization for black-box models, including when training directly against the final model would be costly.
icml-2026-how-to-train-your-advisor-stee.tldr: Small trainable advisor models generate request-specific advice that improves black-box language models across several evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Interpretability researchers often use sparse autoencoders to find meaningful features because a model’s concepts need not correspond to individual neurons. This paper investigates how much useful structure is already available in the original MLP neurons. Empirically, the authors find that these neurons can provide a feature basis as sparse as sparse autoencoders.

They turn that finding into an end-to-end gradient-based attribution pipeline that traces circuits directly through MLP neurons. The pipeline identifies neurons with causal influence on model behavior across several tasks. This matters because tracing can operate on the existing network without the additional training costs associated with learning a separate feature decomposition.

On a subject–verb agreement benchmark, a circuit of roughly one hundred neurons is sufficient to control model behavior. On a city–state–capital task requiring multiple reasoning steps, small neuron groups encode intermediate operations such as mapping a city to its state. Steering these groups changes the output. The results demonstrate concrete cases where individual-neuron circuits expose meaningful, causally effective computation.
icml-2026-language-model-circuits-are-sp.tldr: The authors trace sparse, causally effective language-model circuits directly through MLP neurons without training an additional feature decomposition.

paragraphs: Small recursive models repeatedly update hidden representations to solve reasoning problems. One explanation for their success is that repetition effectively adds network depth. However, recursive models can underperform one-pass models with the same feed-forward depth, suggesting that some repeated steps contribute little useful computation. This paper asks what makes a recursive step productive.

The authors formalize latent reasoning through classifier-free guidance and policy improvement. This perspective treats recursive computation as an algorithm that can improve the model’s decisions, giving a different account of its benefits than depth alone. It also motivates importing training schemes from reinforcement learning and diffusion methods to make repeated updates more effective.

Using the Tiny Recursive Model as their testbed, the authors report that their modifications avoid unproductive steps and reduce total forward passes by a factor of eighteen while maintaining performance. The result demonstrates a substantial efficiency gain in that setting. More broadly, the analysis provides a way to reason about when extra latent computation improves an answer and how training can encourage that improvement.
icml-2026-latent-reasoning-in-trms-is-se.tldr: Viewing latent recursion as policy improvement motivates training changes that cut Tiny Recursive Model forward passes eighteenfold while maintaining performance.

paragraphs: A language model can answer a question correctly and fail when the same meaning appears in a different format or paraphrase. This paper targets such model-specific instability by examining where reasoning changes across equivalent inputs. Its starting point is the model’s intermediate solution process, which can reveal recurring patterns behind rewrite-induced errors.

For each target model, the method samples multiple solution traces under question rewrites and combines recurring intermediate steps into a graph. The graph helps locate where incorrect traces separate from correct ones. The authors then generate a small collection of meaning-preserving examples reflecting the rewrite patterns most responsible for those divergences, using them through fine-tuning or in-context learning.

The approach produces consistent gains across MMLU-Pro, Big-MATH, and DROP, including generalization across datasets. On Humanity’s Last Exam, two hundred in-context examples raise GPT-5.2 with xhigh reasoning from 35.4% to 38.1%. This demonstrates that examples targeted to observed reasoning failures can improve an API-accessible closed model without requiring access to its weights.
icml-2026-learning-rewrite-invariant-rea.tldr: Targeted examples drawn from rewrite-induced reasoning failures improve robustness through either fine-tuning or in-context learning.

paragraphs: Learning against an adaptive opponent is difficult when the environment’s state is only partially visible. The learner must infer hidden dynamics while recognizing that an opponent may respond differently to different strategies. This paper studies partially observable Markov games using policy regret, a comparison that accounts for such strategy-dependent opponent behavior.

The proposed algorithm combines optimistic maximum-likelihood learning with geometrically growing epochs. It chooses one policy for each epoch and builds confidence sets using accumulated observations. Holding policies over these periods keeps the cost of comparing opponent responses across policies logarithmic in the interaction count. For fixed problem parameters, the resulting policy regret grows as the square root of that count, up to logarithmic factors.

The bounds explicitly account for horizon, adversary memory, confidence radius, and a complexity measure called aggregate Eluder dimension. A lower bound matches the square-root and dimension dependence up to problem-dependent and logarithmic factors. Extensions cover horizon-adaptive guarantees and opponents whose memory fades geometrically. The results characterize achievable performance while retaining explicit dependence on properties of the game and opponent.
icml-2026-minimax-optimal-policy-regret-.tldr: An epoch-based optimistic algorithm achieves near-matching upper and lower policy-regret rates in partially observable games with adaptive opponents.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can struggle with precise visual relationships even when their broader image understanding is strong. Procedurally Generated Tasks, or PGT, supplies additional supervision by overlaying clear geometric primitives on images. The framework serves both as training data and as an inexpensive diagnostic for locating sources of perception failures.

The overlays help separate visual grounding from semantic expectations about image content. This lets the tasks emphasize what the model actually perceives about relationships, quantities, and depth. The authors evaluate the approach across diverse architectures and benchmarks covering relational, quantitative, and three-dimensional or depth understanding, testing whether the added supervision improves these fine-grained capabilities.

Augmenting LLaVA-v1.5-Instruct with PGT yields reported improvements up to 20% on What’sUp and 13.3% on CV-Bench-2D while maintaining general perception capabilities. Fine-tuning state-of-the-art models yields gains up to 5.5% and 8.3%, respectively. These findings indicate that inadequate supervision explains many spatial reasoning deficits, making training signals a productive target for improvement alongside questions about architecture or image resolution.
icml-2026-pgt-procedurally-generated-tas.tldr: Geometric overlays provide targeted visual supervision that improves fine-grained perception and helps diagnose multimodal model failures.

paragraphs: Embedding methods represent relationships using points in a chosen number of dimensions. Reducing that number saves representational space, but this paper proves that dimensionality reduction can encounter a sharp accuracy barrier. The analysis uses contrastive triplets, each specifying that an anchor should be closer to a positive example than to a negative one.

The authors establish an information-theoretic obstruction for triplets realizable in an unknown ground-truth dimension D. Their result identifies a constant c below one for which embeddings restricted to at most cD dimensions can be forced to violate almost half the comparisons. In these hard cases, accuracy falls to the level of a trivial one-dimensional solution that ignores the input.

A separate computational result assumes the Unique Games Conjecture. Under that assumption, even nearly one-dimensional realizable triplets can present a problem where no polynomial-time algorithm exceeds the trivial 50% accuracy baseline, regardless of its output dimension. The two results distinguish representational limits from computational limits: increasing dimension addresses the former constraint but does not remove the latter conditional hardness result.
icml-2026-provable-accuracy-collapse-in-.tldr: The paper proves sharp dimensionality barriers for triplet embeddings and a separate computational hardness result conditional on the Unique Games Conjecture.

paragraphs: Some intervention decisions require knowing who benefits more, without needing an exact numerical benefit for each person. Prioritizing preventive care or advertising recipients are examples. Rank-Learner addresses this objective directly, learning an ordering of treatment effects from observational data instead of first estimating every conditional average treatment effect.

The method uses two stages and a pairwise learning objective designed to recover the true effect ordering. The authors show that precise effect estimation solves a harder problem than ranking requires. They also establish Neyman orthogonality, a property that makes the ranking procedure robust to estimation errors in auxiliary quantities, called nuisance functions, used by the learner.

Rank-Learner is model-agnostic, allowing the underlying predictor to be instantiated with different machine learning models, including neural networks. In the reported experiments, it consistently outperforms standard conditional-effect estimators and ranking methods without orthogonality. The contribution is a learning objective and theoretical framework aligned with prioritization itself, together with evidence that this alignment improves the rankings produced in practice.
icml-2026-rank-learner-orthogonal-rankin.tldr: Rank-Learner directly ranks treatment effects using an orthogonal pairwise objective that is robust to nuisance-estimation errors.

paragraphs: RedDebate uses multiple language models to examine one another’s reasoning and uncover unsafe behavior. The motivation is that human evaluation can be expensive, while assessment by an isolated model can overlook problems. The framework organizes collaborative argumentation across diverse debate scenarios as an automated form of red-teaming.

The method also includes separate long-term memory modules that retain safety-relevant insights from debate interactions. Those insights are used during later inference, so the framework can carry lessons from earlier discussions into subsequent responses. Debate supplies critical examination of behavior, while memory provides a mechanism for preserving what that examination reveals over time.

Across safety benchmarks and a diverse set of models, the authors report substantial reductions in unsafe outputs. Debate alone improves behavior, and adding memory produces further significant reductions. These findings support both components of the framework: models can identify useful safety corrections through interaction, and retaining those corrections improves the reported results. The demonstrated outcome is reduced unsafe behavior in the evaluations, rather than a guarantee that every response is safe.
icml-2026-reddebate-safer-responses-thro.tldr: RedDebate combines automated multi-model safety debates with persistent memory, reducing unsafe outputs in benchmark evaluations.

paragraphs: Bayes-assisted conformal prediction combines prior information with prediction sets that have frequentist coverage guarantees. A poorly matched Bayesian working model need not invalidate coverage, but it can make those sets unnecessarily large. RoBAS addresses this efficiency problem by making the score used to construct prediction sets adapt to the reliability of prior information.

The authors provide two versions: one based on a heavy-tailed Bayesian working model and another using a closed-form empirical Bayes shrinkage score. When the prior is informative, these scores use it to produce efficient sets. When that information is weak or inaccurate, they revert to Distance-To-Average, a robust baseline that does not rely on informative prior knowledge.

Evaluations cover tabular and image regression, including settings where training data differ in distribution from calibration and test data. Calibration and test observations remain exchangeable, an important condition in the evaluated setup. The proposed scores are competitive without distribution shift and substantially reduce interval widths in shifted settings. The result improves the usefulness of uncertainty sets while preserving the conformal framework’s coverage role.
icml-2026-robust-bayes-assisted-conforma.tldr: RoBAS adapts conformal scores to prior reliability, reducing interval widths under evaluated shifts while retaining conformal coverage.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models have improved in generation quality, but conventional versions commonly require fixed-length outputs and cannot use key-value caching. Block diffusion introduces left-to-right generation of token groups, yet still fixes their size and sequence. Set diffusion expands this design space by allowing flexible groups of token positions and lengths.

The approach combines a likelihood factorization over token sets with a set-causal diffusion architecture. Its architecture supports key-value cache updates after every inference step, allowing previously computed information to be reused. Since sets can occupy arbitrary positions, decoding can follow different orders, including sliding windows, rather than depending on a sequence of fixed blocks.

The authors report better speed–quality tradeoffs than prior diffusion language models on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation. They also find stronger infilling performance than block diffusion. These results show why the grouping and ordering of tokens matter for both efficiency and flexibility: the model can organize generation around different sets while retaining a mechanism for reusing computation.
icml-2026-set-diffusion-interpolating-to.tldr: Set diffusion generates flexible token sets with per-step caching, improving reported speed–quality tradeoffs and infilling performance.

paragraphs: Speech-in, speech-out dialogue models can respond naturally but may lack reliable factual grounding. External tools can supply information, yet waiting for tool results adds delay to spoken conversation. Stream RAG tackles this timing problem by predicting retrieval queries while the user is still speaking, allowing tool use to overlap with incoming speech.

The authors develop a post-training pipeline that teaches the model when to call tools and how to turn retrieved text into spoken summaries. This links retrieval timing with grounded response generation. They also construct AudioCRAG by converting queries from the public CRAG dataset into speech, providing a benchmark for evaluating question answering in this setting.

Stream RAG improves AudioCRAG question-answering accuracy by more than twenty percentage points. It also achieves state-of-the-art performance on SLUE-SQA, including outperforming cascaded systems, and reduces latency by up to 57%. The framework can also operate on typed input. Its main contribution is making retrieval part of the ongoing interaction, with reported improvements in both factual accuracy and responsiveness.
icml-2026-stream-rag-instant-and-accurat.tldr: Stream RAG starts tool queries during user speech, improving spoken question answering while reducing latency by up to 57%.

paragraphs: Retrieval queries share an embedding space, so their outcomes can be coupled even when evaluation treats them separately. This paper studies how dense collections serving majority interests can crowd out nearby minority content. For example, documents about generic crime movies can occupy retrieval neighborhoods needed to find film noir material.

The authors formalize these interactions as goal collisions. In their static analysis of a fixed embedding space, increasing majority-goal density causes a phase transition in which minority-goal performance collapses. The mechanism concerns which documents occupy the limited top-k results: spatial competition can undermine retrieval for one group as coverage for another becomes denser.

The paper then models document embeddings changing as an agent maximizes retrieval accuracy. A nonlinear Fokker–Planck equation describes this evolution. Within that dynamic framework, the authors prove that the local relevance objective drives self-organization toward a state serving only majority interests. The analysis provides a theoretical account of how a retrieval system’s shared geometry and update objective can jointly produce marginalization.
icml-2026-the-crowded-embedding-space-a-.tldr: A theoretical retrieval model shows how embedding-space crowding and relevance-driven updates can marginalize minority interests.

paragraphs: Test prediction variance, or TPV, measures how a trained model’s outputs respond to small parameter perturbations at first order. The paper expresses it through a trace that separates model geometry from perturbation covariance. This provides one framework for studying effects associated with SGD noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning.

The analysis recovers the wide-minima view for SGD and quantization noise, while label noise leads to a distinct characterization based on Jacobian spectra and a connection to benign overfitting. The authors also prove that training-input TPV approaches test-input TPV in the overparameterized limit, irrespective of generalization performance. Thus, estimating local prediction sensitivity from training inputs need not depend on good generalization.

Empirically, the agreement between training and test TPV extends to much narrower networks than the theoretical limit suggests. TPV also correlates well with test loss. The authors use it to derive JBR, a label-free pruning criterion matching state-of-the-art baselines, and a training-set model-selection signal for both in-distribution and transfer settings. These applications turn perturbation geometry into practical information for post-training decisions.
icml-2026-tpv-parameter-perturbations-th.tldr: TPV unifies local parameter-perturbation sensitivity and supports training-input estimates useful for pruning and model selection.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained multimodal model can improve task specialization while eroding robustness outside the training distribution. This paper develops a theoretical framework for contrastive fine-tuning to study that forgetting. Closed-form solutions and a geometric decomposition indicate that self-distillation retains pretrained knowledge more effectively than the other regularization approaches considered.

The analysis identifies collapse in standard exponential-moving-average teachers used for robust fine-tuning. The authors prove that a weighted-moving-average teacher maintains a regularizing influence over finite horizons. Within their framework, it also permits bias-free convergence in the task subspace while preserving knowledge in orthogonal directions, giving a geometric account of how adaptation and retention can coexist.

These findings motivate TRACER, which combines contrastive learning with weighted-average-teacher guidance through multiple distillation perspectives. Experiments on CLIP fine-tuning show consistent gains in out-of-distribution accuracy and calibration across three backbone architectures. Ablations also support robustness to hyperparameter choices. The contribution connects a specific failure of the teacher mechanism to a theoretically motivated replacement and empirical improvements in preserving useful pretrained behavior.
icml-2026-tracer-persistent-regularizati.tldr: TRACER uses a weighted-moving-average teacher to sustain regularization and improve out-of-distribution accuracy and calibration during CLIP fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Video tokenizers determine both how much information is compressed and how that information is arranged for later generation. Standard three-dimensional token grids represent local details throughout space and time. VideoFlexTok instead produces a variable-length sequence organized from coarse information to finer detail, changing what a downstream model must predict first.

Early tokens emerge as carriers of information such as semantics and motion, while later tokens add detail. A generative flow decoder reconstructs realistic videos from any token count. This lets the representation budget adapt to downstream needs and allows longer videos to fit within budgets that would constrain a grid-based representation.

On class- and text-conditioned video generation, the authors report more efficient training and comparable quality by gFVD and ViCLIP Score using a 1.1-billion-parameter model versus a 5.2-billion-parameter model. They also train a text-to-video model on ten-second, eighty-one-frame videos represented by just 672 tokens, eight times fewer than a comparable grid tokenizer. The findings connect representation order and flexibility to lower downstream modeling costs.
icml-2026-videoflextok-flexible-length-c.tldr: VideoFlexTok organizes variable-length video tokens from coarse to fine, enabling comparable generation quality with a roughly fivefold smaller model.

paragraphs: Weight-space learning represents entire neural networks through their parameters so those representations can support downstream tasks. WeightCLIP adds information about the datasets on which the networks were trained. The motivation is that a model representation becomes more useful when its organization reflects the data associated with that model.

The method uses an autoencoder to encode neural-network weights and a separate encoder to represent dataset samples. A contrastive objective aligns these two kinds of representation, reshaping the weight-space latent space according to dataset information. This establishes a connection between descriptions derived from data and representations that can be decoded back into model weights.

The authors demonstrate applications in retrieval, model generation, and refinement. In particular, dataset information can be mapped into a weight representation that decodes into a strong model. They also introduce a latent refinement process that outperforms standard fine-tuning in their reported results. The contribution is showing that explicitly aligning datasets and model weights expands what learned weight representations can accomplish.
icml-2026-weightclip-aligning-datasets-a.tldr: WeightCLIP aligns dataset and neural-network representations to improve model retrieval, generation, and latent-space refinement.

paragraphs: This paper studies why deterministic and stochastic diffusion samplers can differ in their tendency to generate hallucinations. It compares DDIM’s deterministic reverse dynamics with DDPM’s stochastic reverse dynamics using a Gaussian mixture target. That setting allows the authors to analyze how samples move relative to distinct modes of the target distribution.

The theoretical result identifies a critical time after which DDIM can become trapped on the segment joining the two nearest modes. DDPM’s added randomness helps trajectories escape that region. The distinction is therefore tied to a particular part of the reverse process and a particular geometric trap, with stochasticity providing a mechanism for becoming unstuck.

Empirical validation finds a significantly lower hallucination rate for DDPM when trajectories enter this region. Building on that observation, the authors show how adding stochastic steps can help DDIM avoid hallucinations. The work connects a conditional failure mechanism to a possible sampler improvement: introducing randomness at useful points can change how reverse trajectories leave problematic regions.
icml-2026-why-ddim-hallucinates-more-tha.tldr: For a Gaussian mixture target, stochasticity helps diffusion trajectories escape a region where deterministic DDIM can become trapped.

paragraphs: Off-policy learning derives a policy from previously collected interactions, creating challenges when the learned policy visits different situations from those represented in the data. Zero-shot reinforcement learning adds another requirement: training uses reward-free data, and the agent must adapt to new tasks at test time without further training. This paper connects the two problems theoretically.

The key connection links successor measures with stationary density ratios. These ratios express a correction between visitation distributions, allowing the algorithm to infer optimal importance-sampling ratios for a new task on the fly. Through this mechanism, it performs stationary-distribution correction associated with an optimal policy while retaining the zero-shot setting’s training-free adaptation requirement.

The method integrates into forward-backward representation frameworks. The authors benchmark it on SMPL Humanoid motion tracking, ExoRL continuous control, and long-horizon OGBench tasks. Its central contribution is a way to incorporate off-policy correction into representations designed for rapid task adaptation. This connects the treatment of distribution mismatch with the ability to reuse reward-free experience for new objectives.
icml-2026-zero-shot-off-policy-learning-.tldr: A connection between successor measures and stationary density ratios enables off-policy correction for training-free adaptation to new tasks.
